title: Henry II, Becket and the Angry Words
text:
Thomas Becket rose to power as the friend and chancellor of King Henry II of England. The two hunted, worked and feasted together. In 1162 Henry made him Archbishop of Canterbury, expecting a loyal ally at the head of the English Church. Instead Becket became a fierce defender of the Church's rights against the king. Their friendship turned to bitter enmity, and Becket spent six years in exile.

In 1170 a fragile peace allowed Becket to return. Almost at once he excommunicated bishops who had supported the king. News reached Henry at his court in Normandy at Christmas. Contemporary chroniclers report that he flew into a rage and cried out against the men he had fed and promoted who let him be mocked by a low-born clerk. The famous line about a "turbulent priest" comes from later retellings.

Four knights took his words as a command. They crossed to England and on December 29, 1170, killed Becket in Canterbury Cathedral. The monk Edward Grim, who tried to protect him and was wounded, wrote an eyewitness account. Europe was horrified. Becket was made a saint in 1173, and in 1174 Henry did public penance at his tomb.
lesson: Words spoken in anger by someone with power can be taken as orders. If people act on what you say, choose your words as if they will.
people: Henry II of England, Thomas Becket, Edward Grim
source: Edward Grim, Life of St. Thomas; contemporary chroniclers including William FitzStephen
caveat: The king's exact words are uncertain, and whether he truly meant to order the killing is debated.
